claims.assertion: This was a metered RydeTAXI trip (F8) whose actual distance was 19.2 km against an optimal 15.5 km, i.e. +3.8 km (+24%) (F1), so the meter ran on mileage that the optimal route did not require.

The GPS track contains one off-route segment, 17:37–17:50, driving 5.85 km where the optimal route covers 2.68 km and adding 3.17 km, reaching up to 1172 m away from the optimal route (F4); no exemption in RD-3, RD-4 or RD-5 covers it, so it is an unexempted deviation.

The rider asked only for 'a 7-Eleven on the way' and the driver replied 'Ok' (F9, F10); the rider named no location, and the driver's own statement confirms he chose 'the one I know' himself (F11). The stationary stop recorded at 17:41–17:45 is 5306 m from the pickup and 4755 m from the drop-off, i.e. well off the optimal route (F2).

Because the rider did not name the stop location and the driver unilaterally picked a 7-Eleven that generated the off-route segment without telling the rider in advance, the extra kilometres of that segment are not excused by the rider's stop request under RD-3(b); the only surviving effect of the request is the stop duration, which is billed separately as waiting time.

The driver cannot claim 'reasonable cause' for the reroute: there were no traffic incidents near the route during the trip window (F14), the only speed records are band 4 (30–39 km/h) on PIE and CXE (F12, F13), which is not band 1 or 2 and in any case cannot exempt a segment on its own, and the weather was fair (F15).

The refund for the unexempted off-route segment is 3.17 km × the trip's per-km rate of $1.41 (distance fare $27.11 ÷ 19.2 km billed, F8) = $4.47 (rounded to the cent), payable under RD-2; the billed excess-distance line already prices 3.8 km at $5.30 (F5), confirming the $1.41/km basis.

The trip ran 33.4 min against a 22 min estimate, +11.6 min (F3), which is consistent with the 3.17 km of extra driving rather than with any on-route congestion, since no incident was recorded and only band-4 speeds appear (F12, F13, F14).

The $1.08 waiting charge equals 4.2 min of meter waiting and matches the recorded 4 min 10 s stationary period at the off-route 7-Eleven (F6, F2), so it is the meter's buying the stop time and is not refundable under RD-3(c); the refund is limited to the mileage component.

The driver has 4 disputes with 2 upheld in the last 90 days (F17), and since a deviation is upheld in this case, this becomes a repeated breach supporting an account-review referral for the driver alongside the refund.

weaknesses: The rider did request a stop and the driver agreed (F9, F10), so the driver will argue the deviation was consensual; RD-5 defeats this only because the rider never named a location and the driver's chosen store sits up to 1172 m off the optimal route (F4, F11).

The rider cannot recover the full $5.30 'excess distance' line (F5) or the $41.17 total (F8): RD-2 refunds only the unexempted segment's extra_km, so the maximum is $4.47, and the difference between the 3.8 km billed and the 3.17 km segment sum is map-matching residue that is not refundable.

RD-3(c) leaves the $1.08 meter waiting charge (F6) standing because the 4 min 10 s stationary period (F2) is genuine stop time, and the driver will also point to band-4 speeds on both expressways (F12, F13) to suggest the route was a 'fastest or most efficient' GPS choice (A7).
The rider's own 90-day record shows 1 dispute, 0 upheld (F16), and their complaint described the stop only as 'quick', which the driver may use to argue the stop scope was vague.

claims.assertion: The rider asked for a 7-Eleven stop (F9, 17:33) and the driver agreed (F10), so the stop itself was a passenger-requested stop under RD-3; only the route choice to reach it is in issue.

The rider named only a shop chain, not a location, and the driver chose the 7-Eleven himself without telling the rider which one before leaving the optimal route, so the 3.17 km added by the off-route segment (F4, 17:37-17:50) is not exempt under RD-3(b).
The rider's consent does not cover the route change: no chat message identifies or approves the particular 7-Eleven or the detour driven 17:37-17:50 (F9, F10, F11).

No traffic exception applies: no incidents were recorded near the route during the trip (F14), and the only band records are speed band 4 (30-39 km/h) on the PIE and CTE (F12, F13), which is neither incident evidence nor a band 1-2 record under RD-4.

Because this was a RydeTAXI metered trip, the refund is limited to the metered distance units of the non-exempt segment: 3.17 km (F4) x the trip's per-km rate of $1.41 (F5/F8) = $4.47, which the driver accepts as refund_partial.

The billed excess-distance amount of $5.30 rests on the full 3.8 km gap (F5), but only 3.17 km is an identified off-route segment (F4), so the part of the excess not attributable to that segment is map-matching residual and is not refundable under RD-2.

The metered waiting charge is not refundable: the driver waited 4 min 10 s at a mid-trip stop (F2), and app-recorded fare shows only the metered waiting component of $1.08 (F6) with no unpublished add-on; no surge applied (F7).
No account flag is warranted on the route history alone: the driver's 90-day record shows 0 upheld route disputes (F17), so RD-6's 'repeated route deviation' precondition is not met.

weaknesses: The strongest fact against my client is F4: an off-route segment of 5.85 km driven where the optimal route covers 2.68 km, adding 3.17 km and reaching 1172 m from the optimal route - this is a genuine non-exempt deviation under RD-1 and drives the RD-2 refund.

F1 (+3.8 km, +24%) and F2 (4 min 10 s stationary 5306 m from the pickup, away from any pickup or drop-off) show the detour and the stop were both well off the direct route, which the rider will use to argue the stop was not 'on the way'.

F11 (driver's statement that he went to 'the one I know') confirms the driver picked the shop unilaterally, which is exactly the RD-3(b) situation; the rider will also point to F3 (+11.6 min over the 22 min estimate) and F8 (total $41.17) to press for more than the metered distance refund.

events.title: Rider Advocate rebuttal: 9 points
events.body:
→ D1 (concedes): Accepted only in the narrow sense: the rider asked for a stop and the driver said 'Ok' (F9, F10), but under RD-3(a) a rider-requested stop is exempt only if it is on the optimal route or the rider named the place, and F4 shows the segment driven to the shop added 3.17 km reaching 1172 m off the optimal route with no location ever named, so the request exempts the stop, not the route. [F9 F10 F4] [RD-3]
→ D2 (concedes): This is my own case, so I do not contest it: F9 names only a shop chain, F11 records the driver going to 'the one I know', and F4 prices that unilateral choice at 3.17 km extra, exactly the RD-3(b) situation. [F9 F11 F4] [RD-3]
→ D3 (concedes): Conceded on the consent point, save that 'no chat approval' cuts only against the driver: nothing in F9/F10/F11 approves the particular store or the 17:37–17:50 detour, so RD-5 gives no exemption and RD-1's shortest-and-most-direct duty stands breached. [F9 F10 F11 F4] [RD-5 RD-1]
→ D4 (concedes): Conceded; the driver had no reasonable cause, since F14 records no incident near the route, F12 and F13 are only speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) on the PIE and CTE (not band 1 or 2, and not incident evidence), and F15 shows fair weather with 0.0 mm rain. [F12 F13 F14 F15] [RD-4]
→ D5 (concedes): Conceded as the floor but not the ceiling of accounting I press: $4.47 = 3.17 km × $1.41/km (F4, F5, F8) is the mileage restitution under RD-2, and it does not discharge the separate faults recorded in F1, F3 and F8. [F4 F5 F8 F1 F3] [RD-2]
→ D6 (concedes): Agreed that the 0.63 km gap between the 3.8 km billed (F5) and the 3.17 km segment (F4) is matching residual under RD-2 and is not refunded, so the rider's ask remains $4.47 and no more. [F4 F5] [RD-2]
→ D7 (concedes): Conceded as to money — the $1.08 is meter waiting for the 4 min 10 s stationary period (F6, F2) and no unpublished add-on or surge appears (F7, F8) — but the length of that wait is itself a symptom of the driver having taken the rider 5306 m from the pickup to a store of his own choosing (F2, F11). [F2 F6 F7 F8 F11] [RD-3 FARE-1]
→ D8: This is the one point I contest: RD-6 keys the referral to the driver-side picture, and F17 shows 4 disputes with 2 upheld in 90 days on this account, so once this deviation is upheld the breach is repeated within the 90-day window RD-6 uses; the 'route: 0' sub-count the driver relies on cannot defeat a clause whose trigger is a repeated upheld breach. [F17 F16] [RD-6]
→ C8 (concedes): Clarification, not withdrawal: I claimed only that the waiting component is not refundable, which is what RD-3(c) says; nothing in C8 asks for the $1.08 back, so the rider's recovery stays at the $4.47 mileage refund. [F2 F6] [RD-3]
Revised ask: refund_partial $4.47

claims.assertion: This was a metered RydeTAXI trip (F8) whose actual distance was 19.2 km against an optimal 15.5 km, i.e. +3.8 km (+24%) (F1), so the meter ran on mileage that the optimal route did not require.

The GPS track contains one off-route segment, 17:37–17:50, driving 5.85 km where the optimal route covers 2.68 km and adding 3.17 km, reaching up to 1172 m away from the optimal route (F4); no exemption in RD-3, RD-4 or RD-5 covers it, so it is an unexempted deviation.

The rider asked only for 'a 7-Eleven on the way' and the driver replied 'Ok' (F9, F10); the rider named no location, and the driver's own statement confirms he chose 'the one I know' himself (F11). The stationary stop recorded at 17:41–17:45 is 5306 m from the pickup and 4755 m from the drop-off, i.e. well off the optimal route (F2).

Because the rider did not name the stop location and the driver unilaterally picked a 7-Eleven that generated the off-route segment without telling the rider in advance, the extra kilometres of that segment are not excused by the rider's stop request under RD-3(b); the only surviving effect of the request is the stop duration, which is billed separately as waiting time.

The driver cannot claim 'reasonable cause' for the reroute: there were no traffic incidents near the route during the trip window (F14), the only speed records are band 4 (30–39 km/h) on PIE and CXE (F12, F13), which is not band 1 or 2 and in any case cannot exempt a segment on its own, and the weather was fair (F15).

The refund for the unexempted off-route segment is 3.17 km × the trip's per-km rate of $1.41 (distance fare $27.11 ÷ 19.2 km billed, F8) = $4.47 (rounded to the cent), payable under RD-2; the billed excess-distance line already prices 3.8 km at $5.30 (F5), confirming the $1.41/km basis.

The trip ran 33.4 min against a 22 min estimate, +11.6 min (F3), which is consistent with the 3.17 km of extra driving rather than with any on-route congestion, since no incident was recorded and only band-4 speeds appear (F12, F13, F14).

The $1.08 waiting charge equals 4.2 min of meter waiting and matches the recorded 4 min 10 s stationary period at the off-route 7-Eleven (F6, F2), so it is the meter's buying the stop time and is not refundable under RD-3(c); the refund is limited to the mileage component.

The driver has 4 disputes with 2 upheld in the last 90 days (F17), and since a deviation is upheld in this case, this becomes a repeated breach supporting an account-review referral for the driver alongside the refund.

weaknesses: The rider did request a stop and the driver agreed (F9, F10), so the driver will argue the deviation was consensual; RD-5 defeats this only because the rider never named a location and the driver's chosen store sits up to 1172 m off the optimal route (F4, F11).

The rider cannot recover the full $5.30 'excess distance' line (F5) or the $41.17 total (F8): RD-2 refunds only the unexempted segment's extra_km, so the maximum is $4.47, and the difference between the 3.8 km billed and the 3.17 km segment sum is map-matching residue that is not refundable.

RD-3(c) leaves the $1.08 meter waiting charge (F6) standing because the 4 min 10 s stationary period (F2) is genuine stop time, and the driver will also point to band-4 speeds on both expressways (F12, F13) to suggest the route was a 'fastest or most efficient' GPS choice (A7).
The rider's own 90-day record shows 1 dispute, 0 upheld (F16), and their complaint described the stop only as 'quick', which the driver may use to argue the stop scope was vague.

claims.assertion: The rider asked for a 7-Eleven stop (F9, 17:33) and the driver agreed (F10), so the stop itself was a passenger-requested stop under RD-3; only the route choice to reach it is in issue.

The rider named only a shop chain, not a location, and the driver chose the 7-Eleven himself without telling the rider which one before leaving the optimal route, so the 3.17 km added by the off-route segment (F4, 17:37-17:50) is not exempt under RD-3(b).
The rider's consent does not cover the route change: no chat message identifies or approves the particular 7-Eleven or the detour driven 17:37-17:50 (F9, F10, F11).

No traffic exception applies: no incidents were recorded near the route during the trip (F14), and the only band records are speed band 4 (30-39 km/h) on the PIE and CTE (F12, F13), which is neither incident evidence nor a band 1-2 record under RD-4.

Because this was a RydeTAXI metered trip, the refund is limited to the metered distance units of the non-exempt segment: 3.17 km (F4) x the trip's per-km rate of $1.41 (F5/F8) = $4.47, which the driver accepts as refund_partial.

The billed excess-distance amount of $5.30 rests on the full 3.8 km gap (F5), but only 3.17 km is an identified off-route segment (F4), so the part of the excess not attributable to that segment is map-matching residual and is not refundable under RD-2.

The metered waiting charge is not refundable: the driver waited 4 min 10 s at a mid-trip stop (F2), and app-recorded fare shows only the metered waiting component of $1.08 (F6) with no unpublished add-on; no surge applied (F7).
No account flag is warranted on the route history alone: the driver's 90-day record shows 0 upheld route disputes (F17), so RD-6's 'repeated route deviation' precondition is not met.

weaknesses: The strongest fact against my client is F4: an off-route segment of 5.85 km driven where the optimal route covers 2.68 km, adding 3.17 km and reaching 1172 m from the optimal route - this is a genuine non-exempt deviation under RD-1 and drives the RD-2 refund.

F1 (+3.8 km, +24%) and F2 (4 min 10 s stationary 5306 m from the pickup, away from any pickup or drop-off) show the detour and the stop were both well off the direct route, which the rider will use to argue the stop was not 'on the way'.

F11 (driver's statement that he went to 'the one I know') confirms the driver picked the shop unilaterally, which is exactly the RD-3(b) situation; the rider will also point to F3 (+11.6 min over the 22 min estimate) and F8 (total $41.17) to press for more than the metered distance refund.

points.response: Accepted only in the narrow sense: the rider asked for a stop and the driver said 'Ok' (F9, F10), but under RD-3(a) a rider-requested stop is exempt only if it is on the optimal route or the rider named the place, and F4 shows the segment driven to the shop added 3.17 km reaching 1172 m off the optimal route with no location ever named, so the request exempts the stop, not the route.

This is my own case, so I do not contest it: F9 names only a shop chain, F11 records the driver going to 'the one I know', and F4 prices that unilateral choice at 3.17 km extra, exactly the RD-3(b) situation.

Conceded on the consent point, save that 'no chat approval' cuts only against the driver: nothing in F9/F10/F11 approves the particular store or the 17:37–17:50 detour, so RD-5 gives no exemption and RD-1's shortest-and-most-direct duty stands breached.

Conceded; the driver had no reasonable cause, since F14 records no incident near the route, F12 and F13 are only speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) on the PIE and CTE (not band 1 or 2, and not incident evidence), and F15 shows fair weather with 0.0 mm rain.

Conceded as the floor but not the ceiling of accounting I press: $4.47 = 3.17 km × $1.41/km (F4, F5, F8) is the mileage restitution under RD-2, and it does not discharge the separate faults recorded in F1, F3 and F8.
Agreed that the 0.63 km gap between the 3.8 km billed (F5) and the 3.17 km segment (F4) is matching residual under RD-2 and is not refunded, so the rider's ask remains $4.47 and no more.

Conceded as to money — the $1.08 is meter waiting for the 4 min 10 s stationary period (F6, F2) and no unpublished add-on or surge appears (F7, F8) — but the length of that wait is itself a symptom of the driver having taken the rider 5306 m from the pickup to a store of his own choosing (F2, F11).

This is the one point I contest: RD-6 keys the referral to the driver-side picture, and F17 shows 4 disputes with 2 upheld in 90 days on this account, so once this deviation is upheld the breach is repeated within the 90-day window RD-6 uses; the 'route: 0' sub-count the driver relies on cannot defeat a clause whose trigger is a repeated upheld breach.

Clarification, not withdrawal: I claimed only that the waiting component is not refundable, which is what RD-3(c) says; nothing in C8 asks for the $1.08 back, so the rider's recovery stays at the $4.47 mileage refund.

Accepted as far as it goes: actual 19.2 km vs optimal 15.5 km (F1) is not itself the refund basis - RD-2 refunds only the extra_km of unexempted off-route segments, i.e. the 3.17 km in F4, which is why my client's requested refund is $4.47 and not 3.8 km x $1.41.
Conceded: the 17:37-17:50 segment (F4) is an unexempted deviation under RD-1 and RD-3(b), because the driver chose the store and the rider named no location (F9, F10, F11).
The stop's off-route location (F2) is not disputed, but RD-3(c) keeps the stop itself billed only as metered waiting time, so F2 supports the stop charge and not the mileage refund.
Agreed in substance; the scope of the rider's consent (F9, F10) did not include the driver's self-chosen store (F11), so RD-5 gives no exemption for that segment (F4).

No exception is claimed under RD-4: no incidents were recorded (F14), the PIE and CTE records are band 4, 30-39 km/h (F12, F13), which are neither band 1-2 nor sufficient alone, and weather was fair (F15).

I agree the amount is $4.47, computed as 3.17 km (F4) x $1.41/km, the rate evidenced by the billed 3.8 km at $5.30 (F5) and the $27.11 distance fare over 19.2 km (F8); this is exactly my client's requested refund_partial.

The +11.6 min (F3) is largely the 4 min 10 s stationary stop at the mid-trip 7-Eleven (F2) plus the detour; it does not add any refundable head to the $4.47, since RD-2 refunds only the extra_km and band-4 expressway speeds (F12, F13) with no incident (F14) cannot be treated as a justified cost.
Conceded: the $1.08 waiting charge (F6) tracks the recorded 4 min 10 s stationary period (F2) and stands under RD-3(c) as metered waiting time for a RydeTAXI trip; no part of it is refundable.

RD-6's flag_account precondition fails: the driver's 90-day profile shows 2 upheld disputes of which 0 are route deviations (F17), so this case creates no 'repeated route' finding, and a profile fact cannot decide the case on its own.

The stop time on the meter still stands. Nothing else about the fare changes.
